summary: Overall risk is critical: 10 weaknesses found (4 high or critical), and the traffic looks like VoIP.

executive_report.headline: The VPN has serious security flaws and needs to be fixed right away (risk score 80/100).
key_points: The encryption in session S1 is weaker than current standards.
The integrity check in session S1 is weak, so data could be changed without anyone noticing.
The key exchange in session S1 is too weak and could let attackers work out the keys.
The VPN protocol setup in session S1 is old and has known weaknesses.
The VPN login in session S1 uses a shared password instead of certificates.
executive_report.business_impact: If these weaknesses are not fixed, company data could be read or changed, attackers could join the VPN and recorded traffic could be read later. Even though the traffic is encrypted, an observer can still tell that it carries VoIP traffic from packet sizes and timing.
top_actions: Use SHA-256 or stronger (for example HMAC-SHA-256).
Use IKEv2, or Main Mode if IKEv1 cannot be removed yet.

technical_report.protocol_identification: Session S1: IKEv1 Aggressive Mode, ESP Tunnel Mode over IPv4
technical_report.cipher_suite_analysis: Session S1: 3DES-CBC + HMAC-MD5, hash MD5, DH group 2
technical_report.sa_analysis: Session S1: lifetime 172800 s, replay protection off, PFS off, NAT-T off
technical_report.metadata_exposure: Session S1: peer identity is sent in clear and visible to eavesdroppers | Traffic type can still be inferred from packet sizes and timing even though ESP is encrypted
technical_report.compliance_notes: Session S1: fails NIST SP 800-131A and SP 800-77r1 guidance (Encryption, Hash, KeyExchange, Protocol)
technical_report.uncertainty_notes: Session S1: 14 of 16 values observed directly; inferred, not observed: replay_protection (ESP sequence numbers went backwards or repeated across 40 packets, so the sender is not honouring anti-replay); nat_traversal (IKE was seen only on UDP/500 in this capture)

traffic_analysis.metadata_inference: Small, regular packets (about 150 bytes) about 20 ms apart with balanced traffic (50% upstream), typical of a voice call.

findings.explanation: 3DES uses a small 64-bit block, so an attacker who records enough traffic can recover data (the Sweet32 attack).
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F001 (Encryption)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): keyexchange=ikev1
    # required: AES-GCM IKE proposals are only supported with IKEv2
    keyexchange=ikev2
    # was (observed): ike=3des-md5-modp1024
    # if this peer must stay on IKEv1 for now: ike=aes256-sha256-ecp256!
    ike=aes256gcm16-prfsha256-ecp256!
    # the DH group in the ESP proposal also turns on PFS
    esp=aes256gcm16-ecp256!
findings.evidence_basis: encryption: encryption attribute of the IKE proposal

findings.explanation: MD5 is a broken hash; attackers can create collisions and forge data.
findings.recommendation: Use SHA-256 or stronger (for example HMAC-SHA-256).
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F002 (Hash)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): keyexchange=ikev1
    # required: AES-GCM IKE proposals are only supported with IKEv2
    keyexchange=ikev2
    # was (observed): ike=3des-md5-modp1024
    # if this peer must stay on IKEv1 for now: ike=aes256-sha256-ecp256!
    ike=aes256gcm16-prfsha256-ecp256!
    # the DH group in the ESP proposal also turns on PFS
    esp=aes256gcm16-ecp256!
findings.evidence_basis: hash: hash attribute of the IKE proposal

findings.issue: Weak Diffie-Hellman group negotiated: group 2 (1024-bit MODP)
findings.explanation: DH groups 1 and 2 use 768-bit and 1024-bit keys, which are too short and open to the Logjam attack.
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F003 (KeyExchange)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): keyexchange=ikev1
    # required: AES-GCM IKE proposals are only supported with IKEv2
    keyexchange=ikev2
    # was (observed): ike=3des-md5-modp1024
    # if this peer must stay on IKEv1 for now: ike=aes256-sha256-ecp256!
    ike=aes256gcm16-prfsha256-ecp256!
    # the DH group in the ESP proposal also turns on PFS
    esp=aes256gcm16-ecp256!
findings.evidence_basis: dh_group: group attribute of the IKE proposal

findings.explanation: Aggressive Mode sends the peer identity and a hash of the pre-shared key without protection. An attacker can capture it and crack the key offline.
findings.recommendation: Use IKEv2, or Main Mode if IKEv1 cannot be removed yet.
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F004 (Protocol)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): keyexchange=ikev1
    # IKEv1 is deprecated (RFC 9395)
    keyexchange=ikev2
    # was (observed): aggressive=yes
    # keeps IKEv1 peers in main mode during the migration
    aggressive=no
findings.evidence_basis: protocol: version field of the IKE header

findings.explanation: A pre-shared key can be guessed if it is weak, and the same key is often shared across many devices.
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F005 (Authentication)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): pre-shared key (authby=secret)
    leftauth=pubkey
    rightauth=pubkey
    # this gateway's certificate in /etc/ipsec.d/certs/
    leftcert=gatewayCert.pem
    # set to the subject of the peer's certificate
    # then remove this peer's PSK line from /etc/ipsec.secrets
    rightid="CN=peer.example.org"
findings.evidence_basis: auth_method: authentication attribute of the IKE proposal

findings.explanation: Without Perfect Forward Secrecy, anyone who later steals a key can decrypt old recorded traffic.
findings.recommendation: Enable PFS with DH group 19 or 20.
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F006 (PFS)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): no DH group in the ESP proposal, so no PFS
    # adding a DH group to the ESP proposal enables PFS on every rekey
    esp=aes256gcm16-ecp256!
findings.evidence_basis: pfs_enabled: quick mode was readable and carried no KE payload

findings.issue: SA lifetime exceeds the recommended maximum: 172800s (> 86400s)
findings.explanation: The key lifetime is outside the normal range, so a key is used for too long or is changed too often.
findings.recommendation: Use 28800 seconds for the IKE SA and 3600 seconds for the IPsec SA.
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F007 (Lifetime)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): ikelifetime=172800s
    # 28800 s for the IKE SA
    ikelifetime=8h
    # 3600 s for the IPsec SA
    lifetime=1h
findings.evidence_basis: lifetime_seconds: life duration attribute of the IKE proposal

findings.explanation: Without anti-replay protection, an attacker can capture packets and send them again.
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F008 (ReplayProtection)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was: ESP sequence numbers went backwards in the capture, so anti-replay looks disabled
    # 0 disables anti-replay; values above 32 need the kernel-netlink backend
    replay_window=32
findings.evidence_basis: replay_protection: ESP sequence numbers went backwards or repeated across 40 packets, so the sender is not honouring anti-replay

findings.explanation: The peer identity is sent unencrypted, so eavesdroppers can see who is connecting.
findings.recommendation: Use IKEv2, which encrypts peer identities.
findings.remediation_snippet:
# strongSwan ipsec.conf: fix for F009 (MetadataExposure)
# Session S1, 10.0.0.1 <-> 203.0.113.9. Merge into that peer's existing conn section.
conn session-S1
    # was (observed): keyexchange=ikev1
    # IKEv2 encrypts the identity payloads
    keyexchange=ikev2
    # aggressive mode sends identities in the clear
    aggressive=no
findings.evidence_basis: identity_exposed: an ID payload was sent in cleartext

findings.issue: Negotiated cipher suite is not compliant with the approved baseline
findings.explanation: This cryptographic suite is not on the approved list, so the connection does not meet compliance rules.
findings.recommendation: Use a NIST-approved suite, such as AES-256-GCM with SHA-256 and DH group 19 or 20.
findings.remediation_snippet:

    keyexchange=ikev2
    # was (observed): ike=3des-md5-modp1024
    # if this peer must stay on IKEv1 for now: ike=aes256-sha256-ecp256!
    ike=aes256gcm16-prfsha256-ecp256!
    # the DH group in the ESP proposal also turns on PFS
    esp=aes256gcm16-ecp256!
